newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS - Indonesian stocks seen reaching new highs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Indonesian stocks seen reaching new highs.

text.p: Indonesian stocks fell sharply on Tuesday, a day after ending at a record high, but are likely to gain strength in the short term despite political worries still hanging over the market, analysts said.
The Jakarta composite index closed at a record 719.64 points on Monday, eclipsing the previous closing high of 717.47 set on February 27 this year.

The index shed 0.87 percent to 713.88 points by the close on Tuesday, but brokers blamed the fall on profit-taking in blue chips and some tobacco counters. They said the steep 2.47 percent fall in the Dow Jones Industrial Average on Monday had little effect on Jakarta.
"In terms of momentum, it can break another record this week," said Lin Chee Wei, the head of research at Socgen Crosby brokerage, adding that overseas funds were still coming into the market.

Analysts said the completion of the May 29 general elections, which were swept by the ruling Golkar party, had set aside concerns of political instability and re-focused attention on the country's sound economic fundamentals.

"Indonesia is looking quite good in terms of economic fundamentals," said Jos Parengkuan, head of research at Lippo Securities. "We are seeing capital inflows from overseas. Compared to Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand, Indonesia is looking quite good."
Other brokers said they saw the index rising to 800 points in the medium term while the Singapore-based I.D.E.A. consultancy put initial resistance at 720 points and then at 730.
The consultancy said the outlook for the index was firm despite Tuesday's dips and that only a fall below 711 points would subdue the positive mood.

"You are looking at pretty healthy earnings growth and declining, or not increasing, political risk and I think that should be sufficient to keep foreign interest alive," said Stephan Schmidle, an analyst at Kleinwort Benson associate Mashill Securities.
"Domestic investors would also appreciate that the most glaring political issue is out of the way -- the elections."
But Socgen Crosby's Lin said he had not discounted political risk and was quite bearish on a one-month view of the market.

"In terms of frequency, riots have increased quite significantly. The president has not finalised key political positions, like the chief speaker of parliament, and the political struggle is still there," he said.

Lin said the current bull phase was liquidity-driven -- from overseas capital flows and from the increasing number of mutual funds beginning to operate domestically -- and that corporate earnings forecasts did not support optimism.
But Lippo's Parengkuan said 1998 earnings were looking positive, though the first and second quarter figures of 1997 "were not spectacular".
"On a 1998 basis, the market looks pretty cheap," he said.

He added: "If you going to worry about political uncertainty you will worry until the (March) presidential elections. At the end of the day, fund managers have to say that this thing will continue to be uncertain but I can't wait that long."
Parengkuan said, however, that he expected to see some selling pressure in the second half of July, ahead of new margin trading rules which will be effective on August 1.

The capital market supervisory agency, BAPEPAM, has set up new requirements for margin trading in a move to control speculation. Under the rules, only investors with one billion rupiah ($411,520) in assets and 200 million rupiah in annual income will be allowed margin-trading facilities. ($1 = 2,430 rupiah)
